challenges.situation: Your team has a 'blameless postmortem' culture on paper, but in practice nobody shares their mistakes because they've seen others quietly penalized for admissions. The culture doc says 'psychological safety.' What does mechanism design say to fix?

options.text: Make sharing rewarded visibly (praise, promotion points for catching issues) AND make hiding failures costlier than admitting them (discovered-later penalties). Change the payoff structure, not the words.
options.feedback: Mechanism design: change the payoff structure so self-interest produces the desired behavior. Workshops (B) change words, not incentives. Modeling (C) helps but doesn't fix the structural incentive. Removing bad actors (D) treats symptoms. The mechanism fix: make visible sharing rewarded (consequences for good behavior) and make hiding-then-discovered penalized (consequences for bad behavior). When admitting is cheaper than hiding, rational people admit.

options.text: Retrain people on the blameless culture values through workshops and team discussions
options.feedback: Not quite. Mechanism design: change the payoff structure so self-interest produces the desired behavior. Workshops (B) change words, not incentives.

options.text: Have leadership model vulnerability by sharing their own mistakes first
options.feedback: Not quite. Mechanism design: change the payoff structure so self-interest produces the desired behavior. Workshops (B) change words, not incentives.

options.text: Remove the people who penalize others for admissions — the culture will follow
options.feedback: Not quite. Mechanism design: change the payoff structure so self-interest produces the desired behavior. Workshops (B) change words, not incentives.

challenges.situation: Wikipedia has 300,000+ active editors writing 60M articles for free. eBay has millions of honest sellers in an anonymous marketplace. Both work with ordinary self-interested humans.
challenges.question: What force does mechanism design harness?

options.text: Incentives — the systems make good behavior (contributing, being honest) more rewarding than bad behavior (free-riding, cheating) through reputation, visibility, and consequences
options.feedback: Mechanism design fundamentally works through incentive alignment — making the desired behavior also the self-interested behavior. Identity (B), trust (C), and status (D) are all effects of good mechanism design, not the mechanism itself. The underlying force is incentives: the structure makes honesty/contribution more profitable than cheating/free-riding. Status and identity emerge because the mechanism rewards them — they're downstream, not upstream.

options.text: Identity — people identify as 'Wikipedia editors' or 'trusted sellers' and act accordingly
options.feedback: Not quite. Mechanism design fundamentally works through incentive alignment — making the desired behavior also the self-interested behavior. Identity (B), trust (C), and status (D) are all effects of good mechanism design, not the mechanism itself.

options.text: Trust — the platforms created trust through transparency and community norms
options.feedback: Not quite. Mechanism design fundamentally works through incentive alignment — making the desired behavior also the self-interested behavior. Identity (B), trust (C), and status (D) are all effects of good mechanism design, not the mechanism itself.

options.text: Status — contributors gain social status through visible participation metrics
options.feedback: Not quite. Mechanism design fundamentally works through incentive alignment — making the desired behavior also the self-interested behavior. Identity (B), trust (C), and status (D) are all effects of good mechanism design, not the mechanism itself.

challenges.back: Instead of 'given rules, what will players do?' ask 'given desired outcome, what rules produce it from self-interested players?'
Visibility (behavior observed), Memory (past accessible), Consequences (behavior affects future), Symmetry (all parties accountable)
Makes honesty more profitable than cheating: visible ratings + permanent history + direct impact on future sales = self-enforcing honesty
Invisible prices + per-procedure payment + secret rates + diffused consequences = rational self-interest produces waste and opacity

challenges.instruction: Match each concept to its description:

pairs.right: Visibility + reputation = contributing feels rewarding, vandalism feels futile

pairs.left: Paying doctors per procedure instead of per outcome
pairs.right: Misaligned incentive: more procedures (not better health) is rewarded

pairs.left: Making team contributions visible on a dashboard
pairs.right: Adding VISIBILITY where it was missing — free-riding becomes observable
Nudge: changing the default to align path-of-least-resistance with desired behavior
Missing CONSEQUENCES — behavior has no effect on future outcomes, so it degrades

challenges.context: Which response shows better understanding of the underlying dynamics?

scenarioA.label: Changing the game
scenarioA.text: I design systems where honest, collaborative, long-term behavior IS the self-interested behavior. I don't need better people — I need better rules. If the desired outcome requires heroism, I haven't finished the design.

scenarioB.label: Changing people
scenarioB.text: The system would work if people were more honest, more collaborative, more long-term oriented. We need better training, better culture, better values.

challenges.explanation: The stronger response changes the game so that honest, long-term behavior is also the self-interested move — designing better rules instead of demanding better people.

principle.text: Mechanism design is the art of creating rules so that rational, self-interested behavior produces the outcomes you want. You don't change people — you change the game so that selfishness and cooperation point in the same direction.
principle.subtext: The four building blocks: 1. Visibility — behavior must be observable 2. Memory — past behavior must be accessible 3. Consequences — behavior must affect future outcomes 4. Symmetry — accountability must apply to all parties

reflection: In a system that's producing bad outcomes around you, which of the four building blocks (visibility, memory, consequences, symmetry) is broken — and could you fix it?
